cell.label: claude-code
deviations_manifest: Multiple switching is operationalised as any non-monotone choice pattern (a later line returning to the immediate option) in either price list of any of the 20 tasks. This flags 53 of 504 (A) and 54 of 401 (B) completers versus the 49 and 53 the paper reports, so the samples are 451 (A; Control 108, Treatment 106, Substance-Only 126, Rhetoric-Only 111) and 347 (B; Control 179, Treatment 168) instead of 455 and 348. The literal reading (two or more choice changes within one list) flags only 28/29 subjects, so I used the reading closest to the reported counts.

Valuation = midpoint of the switching interval of the iterated price list: x + 0.2*(# future choices in list 2) - 0.1, where x = 2*(# future choices in list 1) - 2 (as in the Qualtrics piping). It is normalised by the nominal future reward R from Table 2, with no capping. Subjects who switch inconsistently across the two lists (list 2 all immediate) get x - 0.1.

Experiment A conditions are not coded in the data beyond a 0/1 'treatment' flag. Batches 1, 2, 4 and 5 are Treatment vs Control (attention-check words 'compounding' / 'funds'). Batches 3, 6, 7 and 8 are the dissected videos: treatment==1 is Substance-Only and treatment==0 is Rhetoric-Only, assigned from the attention-check wording and the test-score pattern described in Section 2.4.

Answer keys: Experiment A key (2,4,4,7,6 | 3,4,2,3,3) reproduces Qualtrics' own score variable exactly. Experiment B compound-interest key is the same; the B control-module key (4,5,5,5,1) comes from the question content in Table C.2 (for the Coca-Cola/Pepsi item, 0.7 = option 5 was chosen).
deviations_stdout: multiple switching operationalised as any non-monotone choice pattern (a later line returning to the immediate option) within either list of any of the 20 tasks; this flags 53 of 504 (A) and 54 of 401 (B) subjects vs. 49 and 53 reported, so samples are 451 (A) and 347 (B) instead of 455 and 348.
cell.notes: Data are raw Qualtrics exports: 8 batches for A and 2 for B. 'Completed' = all 20 iterated price lists answered, which gives 504 (A, including one subject who took part twice and is excluded as a multiple switcher) and 401 (B, after dropping one survey-preview response); both match the paper. Table 4: OLS of the score on a Treatment dummy, Treatment and Control only, iid SEs. Table 7: OLS without a constant of d = -|r_c - r_s| (pairs matched by future reward and delay) on condition dummies, SEs clustered by subject (fixest). Results: the Table 4 differences are within about 0.02 of the paper. B control-group test-score levels match the paper exactly (1.849, 3.078). Deliberative-competence levels are 0.6 to 1.3 points less negative than reported, and the sign pattern and ranking are reproduced. Ten exploratory runs (kind '', no RESULT lines) were used to decode the data layout, the condition coding and the answer keys, and to test alternative definitions of multiple switching and valuation coding (merged-list switching, capped or floored valuations, exact-amount normalisation, other handling of list inconsistencies). None of them reproduced the published deliberative-competence levels and sample sizes together. During these runs, the diagnostic means were compared with values printed in the paper (Tables 4-7, 9, D.1 and D.3), including Table 7 levels. The final specification stayed at the most direct reading of the paper's description. No run hung.
